doctrine:
An allowance granted without legal basis is properly disallowed. Memorandum Circular No. 174 (2009) authorizes only "scholarship programs" for children of government employees "with siblings"; it does not authorize an **across-the-board cash educational allowance** given to every employee regardless of personal circumstances. Such a grant violates Section 17(e), General Provisions, of the 2010 General Appropriations Act (RA 9970) and lacks the presidential approval required by Sections 5 and 6 of PD 1597 and Item 9 of Joint Resolution No. 4, s. 2009. That approval requirement binds even agencies exempt from the Salary Standardization Law, like the ERC.

Every officer whose approval or certification was necessary to release the disallowed amount is "directly responsible" and is an approving or certifying officer under the Madera Rules on Return. This includes one who only certified the payroll list, or who signed in place of an absent superior. But **civil liability attaches only upon proof of bad faith, malice or gross negligence** (Administrative Code, Book I, Secs. 38-39; Book VI, Sec. 43; Madera Rules 2a and 2b). Officers are presumed to have acted in good faith, and bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality. An officer whose only duty was to verify the names in the payroll has no duty to inquire into legality. An officer who certified legality but erred on a **doubtful or difficult question of law** acted in good faith. Badges of good faith here were the absence of precedent, the fact that this was the first disallowance of its kind, and the auditors' own request for DBM clarification. A mere mistake is not bad faith.

The solidary liability of officers found liable is limited to the **net disallowed amount**: the total disallowed amount minus amounts excused or allowed to be retained by payees (Madera, applied). Payees must return what they received under *solutio indebiti*, regardless of good faith, unless excused under Madera Rules 2c and 2d. *Madera* abandoned the *Silang* practice of shifting the whole refund to the approving officers. Amounts received by payees who are not parties to the petition cannot be ordered returned and are treated as allowed to be retained. Here the net disallowed amount was reduced from PHP 7,433,834 to PHP 315,000, the sum received by the nine petitioners.
facts:
The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), whose personnel compensation is exempt from the Salary Standardization Law under Section 39 of RA 9136, granted its personnel in 2010 an educational allowance of PHP 35,000 each, or PHP 7,433,834.00 in total. It was released in three tranches (February, March and May 2010), on top of a PHP 35,000 Collective Negotiation Agreement incentive.

On August 3, 2011, the COA audit team issued Notice of Disallowance (ND) No. 2011-002-101-(10) for lack of legal basis. It cited Section 17 of the 2010 GAA, Item 9 of Joint Resolution No. 4, s. 2009, and a DBM letter stating that there was no legal basis or presidential authorization. Fifteen ERC officials who approved or certified the release were held liable. Before issuing the ND, the audit team leader had asked the DBM whether MC No. 174 or the CNA could justify the allowance.

The COA-NGS Cluster A denied the appeal (Decision No. 2012-013, September 28, 2012). The COA Proper first denied the petition for review as late (Decision No. 2015-387, December 21, 2015). In Resolution No. 2017-452 (December 27, 2017), it found the appeal timely but still affirmed the disallowance. It held the officers who approved, authorized or certified the payment solidarily liable for the entire amount and, applying *Silang v. COA*, exempted the passive recipients.

Nine of the fifteen officers filed four certiorari petitions. Juan, Tomas, Salvanera, Montañer, Baldo-Digal, Gines and Garcia had only certified their offices' payrolls as correct or approved them; Garcia signed in place of his absent superior. Ebcas, OIC of the Finance and Administrative Service, and Cabalbag, a Finance and Management Officer who signed on Ebcas's behalf, signed obligation requests and disbursement vouchers. These certified the charges as "necessary, lawful" and the supporting documents as "valid, proper and legal." The six other officers (Cruz-Ducut et al.) did not file petitions. Each of the nine petitioners had received PHP 35,000.
issues: Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in upholding the disallowance of the ERC's educational allowance.
Whether petitioners, who signed payrolls, obligation requests or disbursement vouchers, are solidarily liable as approving and certifying officers.
Whether the remaining approving and certifying officers are solidarily liable for the entire disallowed amount.
Whether petitioners must return the educational allowance they personally received.
ruling:
**1. No. The disallowance was proper.** MC No. 174 enjoins agencies to provide "scholarships programs for their children with siblings." By its plain text it covers a scholarship benefit only for employees with more than one child. The benefit must be granted under a set of guidelines (a "scholarship program") that identifies the qualified beneficiaries and the amounts. The ERC's allowance was "merely an across-the-board cash endowment given indiscriminately to every personnel of the agency." With no basis in MC No. 174 or any other law, the grant was prohibited by Section 17(e) of the 2010 GAA, which bars allowances "except those specifically authorized by law." It also lacked the presidential approval required by Sections 5 and 6 of PD 1597 and Item 9 of J.R. No. 4, which apply even to agencies exempt from RA 6758.

**2. They are approving and certifying officers, but none of them is liable because the presumption of good faith was not overturned.** Limited participation alone does not absolve an officer. Under Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code, every official "authorizing or making such payment, or taking part therein" may be liable. Under Section 39, Book I, a subordinate is liable for negligent acts even if done on a superior's orders. The payroll certifications of Juan et al. and Garcia, and the obligation requests and vouchers signed by Ebcas and Cabalbag, were indispensable to the release, so all were "directly responsible."

But liability also requires bad faith or gross negligence. Juan et al. and Garcia only certified the accuracy of the list of employees. Nothing showed actual knowledge of the illegality, and their task did not require them to inquire into the legal basis, so not even constructive knowledge could be imputed to them. Ebcas and Cabalbag did certify lawfulness and erred, but a mistake is not bad faith (*Lumayna v. COA*). Badges of good faith existed: no case law yet outlawed an educational allowance under MC No. 174, this ND was the COA's first such disallowance, and the auditors themselves first sought DBM clarification. The legality of the allowance was thus "a doubtful or difficult question of law," and their error was made in good faith. **All nine petitioners were absolved as approving and certifying officers.**

**3. No. The remaining officers (Cruz-Ducut et al.) are solidarily liable only for the net disallowed amount of PHP 315,000.** Under *Madera*, the officers' solidary liability is limited to the total disallowed amount minus amounts the payees are excused from returning. The obligation to return ultimately rests on the payees under *solutio indebiti*, and the rule avoids an undue burden on officers and the government's unjust enrichment.

The COA's absolution of all payees under *Silang* was erroneous. *Madera* (September 8, 2020) abandoned that approach, and no Rule 2c or 2d exception applied: the allowance was not paid for services rendered, and no undue prejudice was shown. But the payees other than the nine petitioners are not parties, so their receipts cannot be ordered returned and are effectively "allowed to be retained." The net disallowed amount is therefore the PHP 315,000 received by the nine petitioners. The reduction benefits Cruz-Ducut et al. even though they did not file petitions, because their liability is intricately related to the petitioners'. The Court applied by analogy the rule on the effect of an appellate judgment on parties who did not appeal (*Government v. Tizon*). The ruling is without prejudice to administrative cases against them.

**4. Yes.** As recipients, each of the nine petitioners must return the PHP 35,000 he or she received, under the principle of *solutio indebiti*.
disposition: The petitions were PARTIALLY GRANTED. COA Resolution No. 2017-452 dated December 27, 2017 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATIONS. (1) Except for the nine petitioners (Juan, Tomas, Salvanera, Montañer, Baldo-Digal, Gines, Ebcas, Cabalbag and Garcia), all ERC officers and employees who approved and certified the educational allowance, as identified in Annex 1-EA of ND No. 2011-002-101-(10) dated August 3, 2011, are solidarily liable for the net disallowed amount of PHP 315,000.00. (2) Each of the nine petitioners is individually liable to return PHP 35,000.00.

bar_questions.q: In 2024, the Bureau of Waterways, whose compensation system is exempt from the Salary Standardization Law, paid every employee a PHP 30,000 "education grant" without presidential approval. It relied on a presidential circular enjoining agencies to provide "scholarship programs for children of employees with siblings." The COA disallowed the grant. Division chief Lito had signed his division's payroll, certifying only that the names listed were correct. Finance chief Mila had signed the disbursement vouchers, certifying the expense as "necessary and lawful." There is no evidence that either of them knew the grant was illegal. No court ruling or COA disallowance on such grants existed before, and the auditor herself first asked the DBM whether the circular could support the grant. The COA held Lito and Mila solidarily liable for the entire amount as approving and certifying officers. Is the COA correct?

alac.answer: No. The disallowance is proper, and Lito and Mila are approving or certifying officers. But neither is civilly liable, because the presumption of good faith was not overturned.
alac.legal_basis: Officers whose approvals or certifications were necessary to release a disallowed amount are "directly responsible" and are approving and certifying officers. Under Sections 38 and 39, Book I, and Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code, as applied in Rules 2a and 2b of the Madera Rules on Return, they are solidarily liable only if clearly shown to have acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence. Bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality. An error on a doubtful or difficult question of law, shown by badges of good faith such as the absence of precedent and of prior disallowance, is made in good faith. A circular that authorizes scholarship programs for employees' children does not authorize an across-the-board cash allowance. (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023)
alac.application: The grant was an across-the-board cash payment, not a scholarship program, and had no presidential approval, so the disallowance stands. Lito's payroll certification was necessary for the release, but his only duty was to verify the names. He had no duty to look into the grant's legal basis, so no knowledge of the illegality can be imputed to him. Mila certified the expense as lawful and erred, but a mistake is not bad faith. No precedent or prior disallowance existed, and even the auditor needed DBM clarification, which shows the legal question was doubtful. With no evidence of actual knowledge, the presumption of good faith stands for both of them.
alac.conclusion: Lito and Mila should be absolved from solidary liability as approving and certifying officers, although each must still return whatever he or she personally received as a payee.

bar_questions.q: Same agency. A year earlier, the COA had disallowed an identical "education grant," and the DBM had written to the agency's finance chief, Nestor, that the grant had no legal basis. Nestor nonetheless certified the new grant as "necessary and lawful." The total disallowed amount is PHP 5,000,000. The COA excused the rank-and-file payees from returning PHP 2,000,000 under a recognized exception. (a) Is Nestor liable as a certifying officer? (b) If so, up to what amount is he solidarily liable?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Nestor is liable because he certified the grant knowing it was illegal. (b) His solidary liability is limited to the net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.
alac.legal_basis: Approving and certifying officers clearly shown to have acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are solidarily liable under Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code and Rule 2b of the Madera Rules on Return. Bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality; gross negligence includes a palpable or inexcusable breach of duty. The officers' solidary liability is limited to the net disallowed amount: the total disallowed amount minus the amounts the payees are excused from returning or allowed to retain. (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023, applying Madera v. COA)
alac.application: Unlike the officers in Juan, Nestor had actual knowledge: a prior disallowance of the same grant and a DBM letter saying it had no legal basis. The badges of good faith in Juan (no precedent, no prior disallowance) are absent. Certifying as lawful an expense he knew had been disallowed is at least a palpable and inexcusable breach of duty, so the presumption of good faith is overturned. His liability, however, cannot exceed what the government may actually recover. Of the PHP 5,000,000 disallowed, PHP 2,000,000 was excused, leaving a net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.
alac.conclusion: Nestor is solidarily liable as a certifying officer, but only up to the net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.

bar_questions.q: Teresa, a rank-and-file employee, received a PHP 30,000 education grant that the COA validly disallowed. She took no part in approving or certifying it. She argues that, as a passive recipient in good faith, she need not refund anything, and that only the approving officers should bear the liability. Is Teresa correct?

alac.answer: No. Teresa must return the PHP 30,000 she received.
alac.legal_basis: A payee's obligation to return a disallowed benefit rests on the civil law principle of solutio indebiti (Civil Code, Art. 2154). It arises from the mere receipt of an undue payment, regardless of good faith. Madera v. COA abandoned the Silang practice of absolving passive recipients and shifting the entire refund to the approving officers. Payees are excused only if the amounts were genuinely given in consideration of services rendered, or on grounds of undue prejudice, social justice or other bona fide exceptions (Madera Rules 2c and 2d). (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023)
alac.application: Teresa's good faith does not matter. The grant was a cash allowance paid on top of her compensation, not payment for services rendered, and nothing shows that refunding it would cause her undue prejudice. Her receipt of an amount the agency had no legal basis to pay creates the obligation to return it.
alac.conclusion: Teresa must refund the PHP 30,000 under the principle of solutio indebiti.

notes: Consolidated with G.R. Nos. 237860 (Ebcas), 237883 (Cabalbag) and 237884 (Garcia). The petitions were filed under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 (footnote 1).
